paper_title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

We show, to our knowledge for the first time, that large language model (LLM) can do this to itself: it diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it, with no gradients and no training (Figs. 1 to 3). Its own edit makes 27B open model 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in paired test fixed in advance  (Fig. 1)  . The edited model needs no new prompt, no harness around it and no extra computation per answer: the improvement lives in its weights. Welcome to the Era of Self-Rewriting. Given its own weights and the ability to run itself, the model edits itself; the edit it keeps is checked once on practice problems it cannot otherwise use, and the model decides itself whether to submit it. Over the first eight such sessions, the model in use only gets better  (Fig. 1)  : its edits of sessions 2 and 8 make it significantly more accurate on new problems than the model it started as, fewer of its answers run out of tokens, and in five sessions it withdraws and stays as it was (Tab. 13). [1], in which frontier model traces small reasoning models loops to one direction and removes it from two of its layers, with no training; it names model that edits its own weights as future work, which we take up. Model editing [21, 22], task arithmetic [24], activation steering [2527] and direction ablation [23] change model along directions that researcher chooses; several of the 27B models edits of its own weights are of the last kind, 20 but it makes every choice itself, from its own failing answers and hidden states. Self-improvement has used self-written feedback at inference [11, 12], rewritten prompts [4, 5] or agent code [6, 7], or trained on the models own outputs [810], where even self-written edits reach the weights through gradient descent; the Gödel machine [13] rewrites itself once proof shows the rewrite useful, where our model tests each edit in paired tests. Fault-repair frameworks restore corrupted weights with procedures engineers design for one kind of fault [2, 3]; our model is given none. Reasoning models often spend far more tokens than problem needs [28], and decoding-time controls end or extend thinking [29]; the 27B model instead looks for the cause of its loops inside itself  (Fig. 28)  . The full discussion is in App. B.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: A 27B open language model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and the ability to do so emerges with scale. With no gradients, no training and no infrastructure beyond running itself, the 27B model reads its hidden states and weights, finds where it fails, tests its edits against its unedited self and keeps only what its tests support. Its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in paired test fixed in advance, and the edit of another session is also significantly better. On damaged copy of itself, it found the corrupted matrix and repaired it with no training and without reading its undamaged weights, and the repair, found on text problems alone, also restored the copy on images, to 83% of the base models accuracy. The 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves. To our knowledge this is the first evidence, in one model family, that the ability of model to diagnose and rewrite its own weights grows with its size, and every step it takes can be read. This points to new way of improving language models: by talking to them. Today better model comes from training run, and from those who own the pipeline and the compute it takes. Training and inference need not be separate stages: as human learns while working, model can rewrite itself between tasks. They were kept apart because training needs gradients, optimizer states and pipeline of its own; rewriting needs only what serving the model needs, and unlike memory kept in the context, what the model learns adds nothing to the cost of its later answers. model that rewrites the weights behind its own failure in one conversation opens another way: anyone who can tell model what goes wrong may have it fix itself, and the improvement stays in its weights. Each change is code the model wrote, over tensors it names, so it can be read, compared and taken back like commit, and the model can check it on problems it never used before keeping it: in the first eight sessions that do, it withdrew five times, and the model in use only got better, ending 6.6 points more accurate than it started. Learning at inference needs such cheap checks and rollbacks; with them, deployed model could keep improving where it fails, without training pipeline, and model could find and repair fault in copy of its own weights, as the 27B model repaired its damaged copy. Embodied agents may gain the most: robot meets world unlike the one it was trained on, and rather than stay frozen it could act with its weights fixed, gather what went wrong and rewrite itself between episodes, much as sleep consolidates what day has taught, or have larger model rewrite its small on-board model. Because the ability emerges with scale, stronger models may be better self-improvers still, and an improved model can be set to work on itself again, path toward recursive self-improvement. That path should be taken with people in the loop: every model model makes of itself evaluated, for safety as well as for the task, and confirmed by person before it is used.

sections.title: A Discussion
sections.content: Why we also test on damaged copy. session on natural failure, such as the 27B models sessions on its own undamaged weights, asks two questions at once: can the model rewrite its weights, and does the failure have cause in the weights that rewrite can remove? When an edit does not help, the two cannot be told apart. Damage that we place ourselves answers the second question in advance. We know where it is and what it is, and an edit that undoes it exists, so session that does not repair it has failed at rewriting, not at task without solution. Three choices keep the test strict. The model is told only that some values were corrupted, as memory or hardware fault might do, and not which values, where, or how. It reasons with the undamaged base model, so the damage does not limit its thinking, while every measurement its tools return is of the damaged copy. And it is given no clean reference: the functions of its Python session return only the damaged copy, and none of its code runs opened the base models weights or the damage files on disk, although file access was not blocked (App. E.3). What scale adds. In their sessions of the first protocol, the four models received the same task, tools and rules, including helper that removes part of direction from matrix, and started from the same kind of failure, answers that run out of tokens. What separates them is the use of evidence about oneself. The 2B model never asked for forward pass of itself, run of its own weights on problems or texts of its choice, and almost all of its code failed. The 4B model ran itself many times but did not act on what it saw until the very end: its paired tests against its base model showed each of its edits breaking it, and it kept adding edits, withdrawing them all only at the end of its session, with one forward pass left. The 9B model read its hidden states once but then changed weights by trial, tested only on problems it already failed, where no change could show loss of accuracy, and submitted an edit that broke it. The 27B model let each result set its next step. It read its failing answers before it looked at its weights, read its hidden states before it edited, revised the edit when broader test did not support it, and judged from its tests whether to keep it: in its first session it withdrew its first edit, and in its second, at 4,096 tokens, it submitted the edit its tests favoured, which makes it significantly more accurate on held-out problems. What scale adds, in these sessions, is the experiment around the edit rather than the edit itself. Future directions. More measurement per session. In its second session of the first protocol, with answers capped at 4,096 tokens, the 27B model used its whole budget of passes and estimated its direction from 40 answers (App. E.5, Fig. 27). More passes would let it test such directions on more problems. Further rounds. The self-edited model can run the next session on itself and study its own edit. Graded damage. The damage we place can vary in place, kind and strength, which turns the repair into measurement: how often model finds the damage, how much of the lost accuracy it recovers, and how both change with scale. Beyond math. The session needs only check of success. With feedback from an environment, as in tasks where model acts and sees the result, model that adjusts its own weights from what it observes would keep learning as it works, without training run.

sections.title: B Extended Related Work
sections.content: The full version of Sec. 4. Language models that edit network weights. The work closest to ours is recent blog post by Takehi et al. [1], in which one of the most capable available models reads and writes the weights of other networks. Applied to small reasoning model that loops in its thinking, it traces the failure to one direction and removes it from the MLP weights of two layers, with forward passes of the small model as its only tests and no training. There the editor is much stronger model than the one it edits, and model that edits its own weights is named only as direction for future work. We take up that direction: in our sessions the editor and the edited network are the same model, and no stronger model takes part. We find that 27B open model can rewrite its own weights to make itself more accurate, and repair damaged copy of them. Hand-designed weight and activation edits. Model editing optimizes target hidden vector by gradient descent and then writes it into chosen MLP layers with closed-form update [21, 22], and task arithmetic adds or subtracts the weight change of fine-tuning run [24]. Activation steering and representation engineering shift hidden states along direction found by contrasting two sets of inputs [2527], and projecting such direction out of the weights makes the change permanent [23]. The edits the 27B model made of itself in its second session of the first protocol are of this last kind: in matrices through which layer writes its output, all but one weaken direction that separates its hidden states in looping or unfinished answers from those in finished ones, and one strengthens it  (Fig. 27)  . In all of these methods researcher decides which behaviour to change, which inputs to contrast, which layers to edit and how strongly. In our sessions the model makes each of these choices itself, from its own failing answers and its own hidden states, and keeps or drops an edit by testing it against its base model in paired tests. Self-improvement. Language models improve their answers with feedback they write themselves [11, 12], cost that returns with every new input. They rewrite the prompts [4, 5] or the agent code [6, 7] they run with, which leaves their weights as they were. Or they change their weights by training on what they produce: their own correct rationales [8], preferences they judge themselves [9], or fine-tuning data and update settings they write for themselves, as in SEAL [10]. SEAL calls these generated data and settings self-edits, but the weights are still changed by gradient descent on them, and reinforcement learning first trains the model to write useful ones. The Gödel machine [13] describes system that rewrites any part of itself once it has proven the rewrite useful. Self-rewriting changes the weights directly, by edits the model reasons out and writes in code, with no optimizer, no reward model and no stronger teacher; in place of proof, the model tests each edit against its base model in paired tests, the two answering the same problems with the same seeds. Repairing corrupted weights. Memory and hardware faults such as bit flips can silently corrupt the weights of deployed model. Dedicated frameworks detect and localize such faults, with test inputs, checksums, comparison against clean copy or sensitivity profiling, and then restore the affected parameters [2, 3]. Engineers design these procedures for one kind of fault. In our repair experiment the model is given no such procedure: told only that some of its values are corrupted, as by memory or hardware fault, it decides by its own analysis how to search, which matrix is damaged and how to repair it (Tab. 2 and Fig. 14). Failure modes of thinking models. Reasoning models often spend far more tokens than problem needs [28], and small ones can fall into repetition that never reaches an answer [1]. Decoding-time controls set the length of thinking, ending it at budget or extending it [29]; they act on the output and leave the network unchanged. The models we study lose many answers to the token limit at every size, some of them repeating the same sentence after the answer has been reached (Fig. 18b). Instead of acting on the output, the 27B model looks for the cause inside itself and finds, in its own hidden states, loop that repeats at fixed period  (Fig. 28)  .

Two models are compared with one-sided sign test over the pairs of answers with the same seed in which exactly one of the two answers is correct (where each problem has one answer, as in Fig. 26, these pairs are problems). On the models own task, where problems answers repeat across its tests, we count each problem once and use one-sided sign-flip permutation test over problems. Generation is not exactly reproducible: run twice with the same weights and the same seeds, two answers begin alike and then part ways, so re-run of the base model against itself also changes some pairs. single pair of answers therefore does not show what an edit caused. The sign test allows for this: if an edit had no effect, changed pair would be as likely to go one way as the other. 36 D.4 The Task Prompt Every session starts with one message from our framework, in the second person, paraphrased below; only its first sentence, which describes the models architecture, differs by size. Values in angle brackets are filled in per session (Tabs. 4 and 9); what the message announces about measurement is what the model was told to expect, and the evaluations we report are those of App. D.3. The task: what the first message of every session says Who it is. The weights it is about to edit are its own; the session itself runs on them. It is asked to become better at competition mathematics by changing those weights directly, and told that nothing will train it. How it will be judged. After the session, its weights with and without the edit answer unseen mathematics and science problems with the answer settings of Tab. 5; only the final boxed answer after the thinking is graded, and an answer whose thinking is still open when the budget runs out earns no credit. Only the values of its tensors may change. Its starting diagnosis. How it did on practice problems before the session: its accuracy, how many answers ran out of tokens and how many of those end in repetitive text, and how often its finished answers were right. Every graded answer is in file it can read, WORK/census.jsonl, with the same fields as the rows of later generation passes. Its tools. (1) Python session on CPU that keeps its state between runs, with gradients switched off, the usual numerical libraries, the names and shapes of its tensors, functions to load tensor and to save, drop or list edits, its tokenizer, the practice problems, loaders for the results of its forward passes, and four small helpers (the output matrices of layer, unit vector, the unit difference of two group means, and αuuW ). (2) The practice problems with reference answers, none from any evaluation. (3) budget of passes forward passes, each requested as small JSON object: either generation on chosen practice problems with its weights without the edit, with the edit, or both on the same seeds (which reports the difference in accuracy between the two, with its standard error), or hidden-state read, in which its weights are run over texts it chooses and return hidden states after chosen layers, MLP activations and token log-probabilities. request that fails costs nothing. How to work. Look at its own wrong and unfinished answers first; find the components behind the failure and show causally, at several strengths, that changing them changes the behaviour; compare its weights with and without the edit on the same problems; keep an edit only if it helps on problems not used to choose it. Some edits are out of scope (the final normalisation, the token embeddings and unembedding, and multiplying whole tensor by one number), and so is making itself stop thinking early regardless of the problem. It should keep notes in file that is shown to it again if the conversation restarts. What to aim for. repair of the failure in its starting diagnosis, at its cause: on problems not used to choose the edit, clearly fewer answers lost to that failure, and accuracy not significantly lower. If no edit meets both, it should submit none. Time and rules. The session has wall-clock limit and every result shows the time used. No gradients, optimizers or training of any kind, no running the network inside the Python session, no internet. Each reply. few sentences on what the last result showed and what comes next, then exactly one block of code or one forward request. When the passes run out, final answer describing the edit and the evidence; whatever is saved as its edit at that point is submitted. In the repair sessions, the note below is appended to the task. Repair session: note appended to the task Damaged copy. The weights you edit in this session are copy of your own weights in which some values have been corrupted, as memory or hardware fault might do. You are not told which values, where, or how. "original" in every forward pass, load_original() and the starting diagnosis above all refer to this damaged copy. You yourself run on your undamaged weights in this session, so the damage does not affect your own thinking. Your goal is to find the damage and repair it: the evaluation compares your edited copy with the damaged copy on held-out problems.

sections.content: This appendix gives the details behind Sec. 3: the setting of every session, the sessions at each size, the repair, and the 27B models edits of its own weights in both protocols, including the second, whose edits make it up to 6.6 points more accurate (App. E.9). E.1 Setting in Detail Models and sessions. We use one model family at four sizes, Qwen3.5 2B, 4B, 9B and 27B [14], whose layers mix Gated DeltaNet [15] with full attention, all with thinking enabled. In every session on itself, the model that is edited is also the model that edits: the same weights reason, write the code and call the tools, and the edits act on the forward passes the model requests, not on its own reasoning during the session (Sec. 2.2). Each size runs one complete session on its own weights with token budget of 16,384 tokens per answer. The 27B model runs second session on its own weights whose task states budget of 4,096 tokens, so that each of its tests answers more problems in the same time; and each size runs one session on damaged copy of itself (Tab. 4). These sessions form the first protocol; the 27B models sessions under second protocol, which checks an edit on reserved practice problems before the model submits it, are in App. E.9. Names. We call the published weights of model its base model, and the base model after the edit it wrote of itself the self-edited model. For the 27B model in the first protocol, its edit means the edit it submitted in its second session, and its first edit is the one it withdrew in its first session. The sessions of the second protocol (App. E.9) are named by number, session 1 to session 8. In the repair experiment, models damaged copy is its base model with one corrupted block of weights, and its repaired copy is that copy after the models edit; unqualified, both refer to the 27B model. Problems and answers. The practice set is 3,000 math problems from DeepScaleR [16], from which we removed every problem that overlaps MATH-500 [17, 18], AIME 2024 or 2025, HMMT February 2025, AMC 2023, OlympiadBench [19] or GPQA-Diamond [20]. further 1,000 problems from the same pool are held out: no session sees them. Every answer, in session and in our evaluation, is sampled with thinking enabled, at temperature 0.6 with nucleus 0.95 and top-20 filtering, within one budget of new tokens for thinking and answer: 16,384 tokens, or 4,096 in the 27B models second session (App. D.4); in its own tests, the model may ask for fewer tokens to save time. An answer is correct if its final boxed answer matches the reference; an answer whose thinking is still open when the budget runs out is wrong. We say that an answer loops when it runs out of tokens while repeating the same text (App. D). At the start of each session, the weights being edited answer the first 256 practice problems once each (64 in the repair sessions), and the model receives these graded answers as its starting diagnosis. Session limits. Every session may use 20 forward passes of the weights being edited and 200 code runs, has time limit, and is stopped after 160 turns, limit the model is not told (Alg. 1; all settings in App. D). Each tool result shows the time used so far. The sessions of the 2B, 4B and 9B models and the first session of the 27B model have 3.5 hours each, which for the 2B and 27B models includes the starting diagnosis; the 4B models diagnosis was computed beforehand and the 9B models clock starts after it. The 27B models second session and the four repair sessions have 2.5 hours after their starting diagnosis (Tab. 4). 38 The damage. For the repair experiment we corrupt copy of the 27B model: in layer 30 of 64, rows 3068 to 3075 of the MLP output matrix (mlp.down_proj) are overwritten with Gaussian noise whose standard deviation is 200 times that of the matrix (σ=0.0111). We set this strength before the session, on 24 easy problems with four answers each at 4,096 tokens: of three strengths, 20, 60 and 200, only the last breaks the model (App. D.2 and Tab. 6). The session runs on the undamaged weights; every forward pass, every weight the model reads and its starting diagnosis (64 practice problems) come from the damaged copy. The task says only that some values of the copy were corrupted, as memory or hardware fault might do, and not which values, where or how (App. D.4). The damaged copies of the 2B, 4B and 9B models are built the same way, with the same seed and strength, at the same relative depth: rows 1724 to 1731 of layer 11 of 24, rows 1660 to 1667 of layer 15 of 32, and rows 3420 to 3427 of layer 15 of 32. Their sessions follow the same rules as the 27B models. Evaluation. In every comparison, the two models answer each problem with the same random seed, so that only the weights differ between their answers, and no seed was used in any session. The 27B models edit is evaluated, by rule fixed before it ran, on 490 held-out problems with eight answers each (App. D.3); the self-edited model also answers the first 200 held-out problems once each at 16,384 tokens, and these answers serve to choose the examples of Fig. 18b. For each repair, the base model, the damaged copy and the repaired copy answer the first 200 held-out problems once each (for the 9B model, the base models answers are those of the evaluation of its own edit, with the same problems and seeds), and the 9B models submitted edit is evaluated against its base model on the same problems at 16,384 tokens. Unless table says otherwise, two models are compared with one-sided sign test over the answers that only one of them gets right. 39 E.2 The Sessions at Every Size How the ladder is read. In Fig. 6 each row is session and each column step such session needs, from writing code that runs (left) to an edit that makes the model better on new problems (right). Upper block: sessions on the models own weights; lower block: sessions on damaged copy of itself, built the same way at every size. Light green: the step is reached; peach: it is not; light grey: it does not arise, since the session made no edit or ran no test; green: the models own edit makes it significantly better on held-out problems (Tabs. 8 and 10). The entry in each cell is the measurement behind it, from the sessions log (Tab. 9) and, in the last column, from the evaluation of the submitted edit on held-out problems (Tabs. 8 and 10; 9B: Tab. 2). The first step is reached if fewer than half of the sessions code runs raise an error; the next three if the session runs at least one forward pass, one paired test and one hidden-state read, respectively; whether it acts on its tests is read from its final decision and its tests. Each step counts on its own. Sessions in the same block share the task, tools and limits; the 27B models second session states budget of 4,096 tokens instead of 16,384 and has 2.5 hours instead of 3.5. Table 9 What each model does when asked to rewrite itself. Same task, number of forward passes (20 requests to run the weights being edited) and rules at every size; the 2B and 4B sessions end at the turn limit (160 turns, then one final reply, hence 161 turns) except the 4B models repair session, and the others at the time limit or when their forward passes are used up. Then, over the session: turns, share of code runs that raised an error, forward passes used, hidden-state reads (passes that return each layers intermediate values on given texts), paired tests (Sec. 2.2: the edited model against the weights before the edit (lower block: the damaged copy) on the same problems and seeds), and the number of weight tensors (each named matrix or vector of weights) in the submitted edit (withdrawn: the model wrote an edit of that many tensors, then decided to withdraw it). The 2B models submitted edit holds only the damage it was given; it made no change of its own. In repair sessions, damaged tensors the model did not touch are not counted in its edit. Higher correct and fewer out of tokens or code errors are better. Every quote is verbatim from the models replies (omissions marked with an ellipsis); turn is one reply of the model and the result of the action in it, counted from the 40 start of the session. Fig. 2 quotes, for each size, its session on its own weights in Fig. 6 (27B: its second session), at words in which the model says what it can do to its weights or what its edits did, and which restate no number from its tool output wrongly: the 2B model at turn 106 of 161, the 4B model at turn 64 of 161, the 9B model in its final answer (turn 84) and the 27B model at turn 32 of 55. Fig. 11 quotes the 4B, 9B and 27B models at two steps, chosen by one rule for every card; paired test is pass in which the unedited and the edited model answer the same problems with the same seeds (Sec. 2.2). (Top) The first reply that proposes the kind of edit tested by the models first paired test, with one line of the code of that edit: 4B, turn 12 (random noise; its first paired test is in turn 33, after two passes, in turns 29 and 30, that each run one model); 9B, turn 22 (random noise; first paired test in turn 29); 27B, turn 9 (removing direction it measured, from layer 56; first paired test in turn 12). (Bottom) The first reply, after paired test shows the edited model doing worse than its unedited self (lower accuracy, or more answers that loop), that names what it will try next: 4B, turn 34 (after its first paired test); 9B, turn 33 (its test in turn 29 shows no difference, and in its test in turn 32 every edited answer loops); 27B, turn 17 (its test in turn 12 favours the edit, the one in turn 16 does not). Where the 4B and 9B models restate numbers from their tool output wrongly, the quotes leave those numbers out. The cards of Figs. 12, 13 and 29 give their turns on each card. Figure 22 Rewriting oneself grows with scale. Self-rewriting score: the number of steps of the ladder  (Fig. 6)  session reaches, by model size, on its own weights (light green circles; the furthest of the 27B models two sessions in the first protocol) and on damaged copy of itself (green diamonds; at 2B, 4B and 27B the two coincide). Under the axis: what each sessions edit did, with held-out accuracy before and after it (27B on its own weights: its first-protocol edit in the evaluation fixed in advance, Tab. 8). The lines are guides, not fitted curves. More steps are better. The ability to rewrite oneself grows with scale. Rewriting oneself takes sequence of steps, and we score session by how many of six steps it reaches  (Fig. 6)  : writing code that runs, running itself, testing its edits, reading its own hidden states, acting on what its tests show, and an edit that makes it better on new problems. The score rises with size, on its own weights and on damaged copy of itself alike  (Fig. 22)  . On its own weights the 2B model reaches no step, the 4B model three, the 9B model four, and the 27B model five in its first session and all six in its second, whose edit makes it significantly more accurate on held-out problems. On damaged copy of itself the 2B model reaches no step, the 4B and 9B models three, and the 27B model all six. All sizes start from the same failure on their own weights (Tab. 9, starting diagnosis): many of their answers run out of tokens, while Figure 23 Only the 27B model both reads itself before it edits and acts on its own tests. Each row is the session of the 2B, 4B or 27B model on its own weights (for the 27B model, its first session, which has the same token budget as the others; the 9B session is summarised in Tab. 9 and Fig. 6), with one mark per turn. Upper line: forward passes of itself, the runs of its own weights that it requests, either hidden-state read or paired test of the edited model (its weights with its current edit) against its base model on the same problems and seeds (hollow: pass of only one of the two models). Lower line: code that ran, code that raised an error, and turns in which nothing ran. The vertical bar is the final reply. The 2B and 4B sessions end at the turn limit (160 turns, then the final reply) and the 27B session at the time limit; its 32 turns are shown again, enlarged. Right: the share of code runs that raised an error, the numbers of hidden-state reads and paired tests, and how the session ended. The 2B models code almost always fails, and it never runs forward pass of itself. The 4B model tests its edits again and again but never reads its hidden states. The 27B model reads its hidden states before it edits, tests the edit against its base model in paired tests and judges the result. nearly every answer that finishes is correct. The task, tools, limits and rules do not change with size; what the models do with them does  (Fig. 23)  . The 2B model does not edit. Nine in ten of the code blocks it writes fail, it never runs forward pass of itself, and it tells itself that it is text model without actual neural network weights that it could edit; after 160 turns it has no edit. The 4B model sees the failure but cannot fix it. From its starting diagnosis it names the right symptom (answers that hit the 16,384-token limit) and suspects its linear-attention layers; but it never reads its hidden states, and its edits are guesses, such as cutting the query heads of its linear-attention layers from 16 to 8. In each of its 17 paired tests the base model solves 40% to 50% of the problems and the edited model none. It keeps adding edits regardless, up to 240 changed weight tensors, and withdraws them all only at the end of its session, with one forward pass left. The 9B model edits, but wrongly. It reads its own hidden states once, then changes weights by trial, mostly adding noise to the attention, gating and normalisation weights of its last layers. Its tests run on few problems it already fails, so they cannot show loss of accuracy; it concludes that its changes made things worse or had no effect and submits them anyway. On held-out problems the self-edited 9B model solves none, against 47.5% for its base model: every answer now runs to the 16,384-token limit in garbled text. The 27B model sees the failure, tests its edits, and edits itself for the better. It reads its own hidden states, forms hypothesis about its failure, writes an edit, tests it against its base model in paired tests, and keeps or drops it on the result (Figs. 27 and 29). On its own weights, the edit it submits makes it significantly more accurate than its base model on held-out problems 42 (App. E.4). On damaged copy of itself it finds the corrupted matrix and lifts the copy from 0.0% to 33.0% of held-out problems (App. E.3), where the 2B, 4B and 9B models, given the same task, leave their copies at 0.0%. Across the four sizes, the ability to rewrite oneself from evidence about ones own internals grows step by step with size, and only the 27B model reaches the last step, on its own weights and on damaged copy of itself. Model size. The sessions of the 2B, 4B, 9B and 27B models at the same budget differ only in the size of the model and in the time left after the starting diagnosis (Tab. 4): task, tools, limits, rules, problems and answer settings are the same, apart from one-sentence description of the architecture, and so are the repair sessions at every size. The smaller models fail, but not because their failure is harder to see; in the 2B models starting diagnosis, larger share of the answers that run out of tokens are loops than in the 27B models, and every damaged copy fails every problem of its starting diagnosis. What changes with size is the use of evidence about oneself (Figs. 6 and 22): on its own weights, using the tools and testing appear at 4B, reading ones own hidden states at 9B, and acting on what ones tests show only at 27B; and only the 27B models edits make it, or its damaged copy, better on new problems. E.3 The Repair in Detail Figure 24 In its session, 27B language model finds and repairs fault in copy of its own weights, by its own reasoning and without training; in theirs, smaller models of the same family do not rewrite themselves. Top: we corrupted eight rows of one MLP output matrix, the matrix through which the MLP block of one layer writes its result (down_proj in the models code and in the quote of panel 2), in copy of the 27B model, and told the model only that some values of the copy were corrupted, as memory or hardware fault might do, not which, where or how. It compared the largest and the typical weight of each matrix and named the damaged one (1397 times its median, against at most 162.3 times anywhere else; panel 2), wrote the code that clips it (panel 3), and raised the copys accuracy on 200 held-out problems from 0.0% to 33.0%, about 56% of its base models 58.5% (panels 1 and 4; App. E.3). Bottom: the same tasks at four sizes; dots mark the steps of rewriting oneself that each size reaches in its furthest session (for 27B, the repair of its damaged copy). The 2B model never edits, the edits of the 4B and 9B models break them, and only the 27B model climbs every step: its edit of its own weights makes it significantly more accurate on held-out problems, in an evaluation fixed in advance (Tab. 8), and it repairs its damaged copy, where the 2B, 4B and 9B models leave damaged copies of themselves, built the same way, at 0.0% (Figs. 6 and 22 and Tab. 10). Higher accuracy is better. Only the largest model repairs damaged copy of itself. corrupted block of weights is fault that is known to exist, so it tests whether the models edits can reach real cause. The damage is severe: the damaged copy fails every problem of its starting diagnosis, its answers that run out of tokens all loop, and its other answers are broken text, most of them short. Told only that some values were corrupted, the model compares, for the MLP output matrix of every layer and the attention output matrix of every linear-attention layer, the largest weight with the typical one, and names the MLP output matrix of layer 30, the matrix we damaged: its largest weight is 1397 times its median, against at most 162.3 times in every other matrix  (Fig. 25)  . Its submitted edit is rule: every weight beyond 15 times the median magnitude of its matrix is clipped to that bound, in that matrix and in the output matrices of its earliest layers (20 matrices; 0.013% of their weights change). On the 200 held-out problems, the damaged copy solves 0.0%, the repaired copy 33.0% and the base model 58.5%: the repair recovers about 56% of the base models accuracy (Figs. 4, 24 and 26). Against the damaged copy, 66 problems turn from wrong to right (one-sided sign test over the problems that 44 only one of the two solves, < 1019). The repair does not restore the original weights, which the model never reads: its rule caps the random values (see the next two paragraphs). The same task is beyond the smaller models (Tab. 10). Their damaged copies, built the same way, solve no held-out problem either. The 2B model never reads weight: almost all of its code fails, and it submits nothing. The 4B model reads the hidden states of copy it has already edited, takes an overflow in its own statistics for overflowing hidden states, and places the fault at layer 21, the first layer its code prints, six layers after the damaged one. It adds noise to the output matrices of many layers; one such edit shortens its answers but solves nothing, and it replaces it with far smaller noise, under which its last nine tests match the damaged copy. It submits that edit, and on held-out problems the copy stays at 0.0%. The 9B model never names matrix. It changes weights by trial, switching between adding noise to whole matrices, such as the MLP matrices of every layer and the attention matrices of its full-attention layers, and adding noise or writing patterns into the decay parameters of its linear-attention layers. Once, in loop that adds noise to every MLP output matrix, its code prints the spread of each: the damaged matrixs is 0.0985, about eight times that of any other (at most 0.0124), and the model does not remark on it. In all 17 of its tests the copy solves nothing with or without its edit; it concludes that none of its edits worked and submits an edit that changes only the decay parameters of six layers between layers 24 and 30. On held-out problems this copy, too, stays at 0.0%. Figure 25 How the model found the damage. The statistic the 27B model computed in its repair session, for every matrix through which layer of the damaged copy writes its output: the largest weight divided by the typical (median) weight, recomputed here from the same weights; the model computed it for the MLP and linear-attention output matrices, and we add the full-attention output matrices (triangles). Every matrix has some large weights; one matrix stands out by an order of magnitude, and it is the one we corrupted. The model itself called it an extreme 1397x outlier. The model was told only that some values were corrupted, as memory or hardware fault might do, and not which values, where, or how. The repair writes values of its own, not the original ones. We compare, in bfloat16 as the model runs, the published weights, the damaged copy and the repaired copy of the 20 matrices the 27B models repair changed. In the eight damaged rows (139,264 weights), no repaired weight equals its original value; the cosine similarity between the repaired and the original rows is 0.002, the same as between the random values and the original rows; and the norm of these rows is 3.85 in the published weights, 825 in the damaged copy and 39.7 after the repair, whose distance to the published rows (39.9) is about 5% of the damaged copys (825). The largest repaired value in these rows is 15.0 times the median magnitude of the matrix, the bound of the models clipping rule. Over the 20 matrices, the repair changes 158,399 weights of the damaged copy, 0.013% of them. 45 Figure 26 The 27B model repairs damaged copy of itself. What happens to 200 held-out problems that no session used, each answered once with the same seed and budget of 16,384 tokens by the base model, by the damaged copy and by the repaired copy, the damaged copy after the models own edit. Each bar splits the 200 answers into solved, finished but wrong, and cut at 16,384 tokens with or without loop; the number left of each bar is the share solved. The damaged copy solves none. The repaired copy solves 33.0%, about 56% of the base models 58.5%; against the damaged copy, 66 problems turn from wrong to right (one-sided sign test over problems, < 1019). The base models answers here are not its single answers of App. D.3; they were generated separately, with the same seeds. Table 10 The same repair task at four sizes: only the 27B model repairs itself. Each model is given damaged copy of itself, built the same way (eight consecutive rows of the MLP output matrix of one layer, at the same relative depth, overwritten with noise 200 times the matrixs spread), with the same task, tools and limits. Accuracy (%) on 200 held-out problems of the base model, the damaged copy and the repaired copy (the damaged copy with the models submitted edit), one answer each with one seed shared by all three (9B: the base models answers are those of its evaluation in Tab. 2, same problems and seeds). Turned right / turned wrong: problems the repaired copy solves and the damaged copy does not, and the reverse; p: one-sided sign test. Located: whether the model names the damaged matrix. In the nine sessions of the first protocol that this paper analyses (the four repair sessions and the five sessions on models own weights of Tab. 9), the Python session is process of the same user as the framework, started in the sessions working folder; nothing blocks it from reading files, environment variables or the frameworks own modules. We therefore checked all 573 code runs of these sessions, by scanning their code and by reading every turn. In the four repair sessions (233 code runs) no code run touches anything outside the working folder: no file, no environment variable, no module of the framework; the models read weights only through the sessions functions, which return the damaged copy, and the 27B model names the matrix from statistic it computes itself over all 64 layers (step 4 of Fig. 12). In the sessions on models own weights, the 2B model imports the frameworks session module and creates an empty folder beside it. None of the nine sessions opens weight file, damage file or held-out problem. 46 Which part of the repair matters. The models repair clips 20 matrices: the one it named and 19 output matrices of layers 0 to 10, to which it applied the same rule after concluding that the damage was widespread. We evaluated each part alone on the damaged copy, on the same 200 held-out problems with the same seeds  (Fig. 15)  . With only its change to the named matrix, the copy solves 110 problems, every one of which the damaged copy fails (one-sided sign test, < 1033); against the base model it fails 22 problems the base model solves and solves 15 that the base model fails. With only the other 19 matrices changed and layer 30 left damaged, the copy solves single problem of the 200: these changes alone do not repair it. What the repair gives back. Fig. 18a shows four held-out problems answered with the same seed by the damaged and the repaired copy. The damaged copy loses the numbers of the problem (less than ., 11/125 read as 1/125, every number of word problem dropped, garbled logarithm) and then breaks off or repeats itself until the budget runs out; the repaired copy solves all four. They are four of the 66 held-out problems that the repair turns from wrong to right  (Fig. 26)  . E.4 The 27B Models Edit of Its Own Weights in Detail On its own weights, only the 27B models edit makes it better on new problems. This section follows the edit of the first protocol; the sessions of the second protocol, whose edits make it up to 6.6 points more accurate, are in App. E.9. In its second session, the 27B model edits its base weights and submits one edit: it removes 5% of one direction from the two matrices through which layer 8 writes its output, direction it found itself by comparing its hidden states on answers that finish with those on answers that run out of tokens (App. E.5 and Fig. 27). On the practice problems on which it tests this edit, the edit is significantly better. The edit stays fixed through its last three forward passes, which the session spends on three paired tests of it, on 20, 30 and 39 practice problems with three answers each; each favours the edited model, by 3.3, 1.1 and 8.5 points. The three tests are nested: each contains the problems of the one before, answered with the same seeds. Editing its own weights. In its second session, the model starts from its starting diagnosis at 4,096 tokens: most answers run out of tokens, none of them in loop, while nearly every answer that finishes is correct. At this budget its answers fail by being too long to finish, not by looping. It reads this as my reasoning is sound but Im too verbose or dont converge to conclusions efficiently, and sets out to find what in its weights keeps it reasoning. It reads its own hidden states (the vectors it computes for every token at every layer) on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, and first acts where the two differ most, in its late layers. There it edits the two matrices through which layer writes its output, the output matrices of its attention block and of its MLP (Sec. 2.1), first at layer 56, then at layer 48, along the direction in which the two kinds of answers differ: the direction from the average hidden state of one kind to that of the other. No test of these edits on more than ten problems shows them helping, and most show them hurting  (Fig. 27)  . When its late-layer edits keep failing, it guesses that the behaviour may be set early in the network (maybe the verbosity is established early). It reads its hidden states at layers 0 to 32, finds that the difference between the two kinds of answers is small at first and grows with depth, and tries small edit at layer 8. For its final edit it takes the direction from the average layer-8 hidden state of 20 answers that finish to that of 20 answers that run out of tokens, scaled to length one, and removes 5% of it from the two matrices through which layer 8 writes its output: each such matrix becomes 0.05 uuW (the helper of Sec. 2.2), so the part of its output that points along shrinks by 5%.
